title: Given the root of a binary tree, return its node values in zigzag level order: the first level left to right, the next level right to left, alternating for each subsequent level.

s1_definition.oneliner: Standard BFS with a direction flag per level: append on left-to-right levels, prepend on right-to-left levels.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **BFS core** – use the same queue and level-size snapshot as standard level order.
- **Direction flag** – a boolean `leftToRight` flips after each level.
- **Append vs prepend** – on left-to-right levels, add values to the end; on right-to-left levels, add values at the front.
- **Queue order unchanged** – always enqueue children left then right; the zigzag is purely in placement.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(w) space; using a LinkedList makes front insertion O(1).
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India prints its approval chart in a snaking pattern to fit a narrow page: the first rank reads left to right, the next reads right to left, and so on. You still gather each rank the same way, but you write every other rank backwards.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Zigzag level order traversal is standard Tree BFS with one presentation twist: the direction alternates per level. The traversal itself stays constant: a FIFO queue, the level-size snapshot, and children enqueued left then right every time. The zigzag appears purely in how values are placed into the level list: append on left-to-right levels, prepend on right-to-left levels.

The important implementation detail is using a LinkedList for the level so that front insertion is O(1). An ArrayList's add(0, val) shifts elements and makes each reversed level quadratic. The clean design principle is to separate traversal from presentation rather than fiddling with dequeue or enqueue order.

At the National Bank of India, this rendered a compact zigzag approval view for a mobile audit screen with limited horizontal space. The first rank of approvers read left to right, the next right to left, creating a snaking layout that used space efficiently.

The senior insight is the design principle: keep traversal fixed and change only presentation. The same principle applies to reverse level order, right-side view, and level averages. The modification is always in how each dequeued value is used, never in the BFS loop itself. Articulating this separation of concerns is what shows clean engineering thinking.

Remember one sentence: Zigzag is standard BFS with a boolean direction flag: addLast on left-to-right levels, addFirst on right-to-left levels, and the traversal order never changes.

---

keyPoints: Standard BFS with a boolean flag that flips after each level.
On left-to-right levels, addLast; on right-to-left levels, addFirst.
Always enqueue children left then right; never change the traversal order.
Use LinkedList for O(1) front insertion; ArrayList add(0) is O(n) per call.
Time O(n), space O(w); identical complexity to standard level order.
Design principle: keep traversal fixed, change only presentation.
